The four frames don't share a visual world. One is a night scene with a VW camper rendered in 3D. One is a flat vector golfer on a cream ground. One is a portrait-format pink convertible floating on cream. One is a glossy 3D mint fridge with a reflective floor. Even the aspect ratio changes, which points to separate generations put side by side, not one designed film.
The pink car is clip-art: a vector-default illustration centred on an empty cream field with no setting.
The golfer is three poses repeated in a stock flat-illustration style (gradient shirt, generic face) with nothing distinctive about them.
The 'I.O.U.' note in the fridge is the only gag, and it reads as a one-line prompt joke with no setup elsewhere in the film.
There is no type system and no consistent palette, so nothing links one frame to the next.
gaps: Commit to one world: one rendering style, one palette and one aspect ratio held for the whole film, the way B keeps its silhouette-and-flat-colour language.
Build a narrative or graphic idea that carries the cuts (a chase, a recurring motif, a match-cut) instead of unrelated vignettes.
Put the subjects in staged environments with motivated light and texture rather than isolating clip-art objects on empty grounds.

tells: The credits are built into the scene: one name is on the park gate's arch and 'ANDY SERKIS' lies in a pool of streetlight on the ground, so every credit is staged inside the world.
Silhouettes are cut against bold flat colour fields that shift dramatically between frames (dusty pink, aubergine, acid green spiral, teal), which gives a deliberate and unusual palette.
The frames clearly show a continuous chase between frames: a high overhead angle down an alley, a vortex spiral, a rooftop, with recurring characters and a little white dog as a through-line.
There's real paper-like texture and graphic shadow play, a 60s caper-title homage with a clear point of view.
The custom geometric caps have a consistent hierarchy ('A … FILM', 'EDITED BY') and are placed with care in every frame.
gaps: The flat ochre credit type could sit a little deeper in the lighting of a few scenes, as the 'Serkis' frame already does.
The vortex frame is busy, so the credit competes slightly with the action.
This is the benchmark entry, so the remaining gaps are marginal.

tells: The concept is irreverent and specific: old, grimy diesel engines are expelled from a saccharine rainbow paradise. The contrast between sweet and gritty is the idea itself.
The type is part of the world: 'HATE' is spelled in topiary and peacock-feather eyes, and 'CHANGE' is spelled on balloons balanced by seals. The lettering is staged as props, not overlaid.
Characters act and things change between frames: a flamingo with a bat swats an engine, a rabbit cheers as engines fly off trailing smoke. There is clear choreography and comic timing.
The deliberately over-saturated palette is used ironically. It's a hyperreal storybook look that matches the tone.
The engines are rendered with dense detail and grime against clean CG nature, a deliberate clash of materials.
gaps: The CG environment lighting is fairly even and dated next to B's graphic control of light.
Compositions are busy and centre-weighted in places (the 'CHANGE' frame), so they lack B's poster-like clarity.
The look is maximalist on purpose, but a tighter edit of the elements in each frame would sharpen the jokes.

tells: The four frames don't share a world. One is a 3D-ish VW van on dark hills, one is a flat vector golfer on a cream ground, one is a centred pink convertible on cream and one is a glossy rendered fridge. That reads as separate generations, not a designed system.
Every subject is an isolated object centred on an empty plain or black ground. There is no environment and no layering.
The golfer is a three-pose strip with a default gradient shirt. It looks like clip art, and the pose-to-pose sequencing shows no motion craft.
The fridge 'I.O.U.' note is the only idea in the piece, and it's a stock gag with no build-up from the earlier frames.
The only type is a scrawled sticky note. Nothing typographic carries the film.
gaps: Commit to a single visual language and world across the whole film, the way B's flat-silhouette Hergé pastiche holds every frame together.
Build each frame as a staged scene with foreground, midground and background and motivated light, instead of a centred object on a void.
Thread one idea through the sequence so that frames hand off to each other (match cuts, transformations) instead of reading as unrelated vignettes.

tells: A specific idea: silhouette chase vignettes that give an affectionate graphic nod to the source comics, with credits staged inside the action.
Type is integrated into the world. 'ANDY SERKIS' is painted onto the ground in a pool of lamplight, and the director credit sits on an ornate park-gate sign.
The palette shifts deliberately each sequence: dusty pink, bruised purple and green, acid chartreuse spiral, teal night. Each is unusual and controlled.
Extreme camera angles (a top-down alley, a vortex spiral, a low horizon) and the shadow play imply strong choreography and variety between shots.
Paper texture, pooled light and cast shadows give it real material depth despite the flat silhouettes.
gaps: The credit typeface is a fairly conventional bold caps sans. A more bespoke lettering treatment could match the image-making.
Some credits, such as 'TOBY JONES', just sit on the frame rather than being staged in the world like the Serkis credit.
The reference to its source is strong but leans on a known genre (Saul Bass-style silhouette titles), so it is less surprising than it is masterful.

tells: A memorable, specific idea: a saccharine rainbow paradise where cute creatures attack and banish clunky old diesel engines. It has a sharp brand point and a twist on the cute genre.
The type is built from the world: topiary letters, a peacock fan spelling 'HATE' and seals balancing 'CHANGE' balloons. Lettering comes out of the scene, not slapped on top.
Escalating narrative across frames: idyll, intrusion, mustering, then the engines blasted off by a rainbow. That's real choreography and a payoff.
Deliberately over-sweet palette used ironically, with grimy realistic engines as the counterpoint material.
gaps: Early-2000s CG rendering: the lighting and materials on the creatures and terrain are plasticky and flat next to B's crafted texture.
Compositions are busy and fairly centred. Frames work as story beats more than as posters.
The irony depends on cliché imagery (rainbows, swans, seals). Tighter art direction could push it from pastiche to a signature look.

tells: The letters are built into the world rather than laid over it: topiary hedges, a peacock's tail feathers, and balls balanced on the noses of seals on plinths spelling CHANGE. That is a typographic idea with choreography behind it.
The tone is ironic and maximalist: rusty engines barrelling through a candy-coloured Arcadia, and a flamingo with a baseball bat. That clash is a deliberate concept, not a style left on default.
The four frames are completely different setups (wide landscape, mid-air gag, a staged lettering tableau, mass destruction), so the piece clearly has a narrative arc.
The CG is of its era and slightly plasticky, with simple GI lighting. The kitsch is on purpose, but the finish is TV-commercial grade, not award grade.
gaps: The rendering is generic saccharine CG. Push the material contrast between the oily, rusted engines and the sugary world so the satire reads in the texture too.
The palette is the default rainbow-pastel. A more authored, restricted kitsch palette would make every frame read as a poster.
The letterform gags are clever but sit centred at mid-scale. Integrate the type with more scale contrast and better camera framing, the way B's credits are built into each composition.

tells: The credits live inside the world: a park-gate sign, a name lying in a pool of street-lamp light, a name in a hypnotic vortex, a credit on a blue skyline. Each credit gets its own staging.
Every frame uses a different, deliberate palette (dusty pink, poison violet, acid green-yellow, teal-indigo), so the colour carries the beats of the chase.
Silhouetted characters, a strong graphic shadow play and a high-angle noir camera with a pool of light. This is evident choreography and cinematic staging.
It has a paper-grain texture, period-appropriate letterforms with real spacing, and a white dog motif threaded through every frame.
gaps: Some name cards use a fairly uniform bold sans. More variation in the type's scale would add punch.
The silhouette-chase vocabulary sits in a well-trodden lineage (Saul Bass, Catch Me If You Can), so its originality ceiling is limited.
The texture is subtle. More print-like registration and grain would deepen the material quality.

tells: There is no visual system. A glossy 3D van on black, a flat-vector golfer on cream, an isolated pink car on a cream portrait card and a photoreal retro fridge share no common style, and the aspect ratios are inconsistent. It reads as unrelated outputs stitched together.
The golfer is default corporate flat illustration (gradient shirt, generic proportions), and the subjects are centred on empty grounds with nothing else in the frame.
The fridge's 'I.O.U.' sticky note is the only idea, and it is a literal visual pun. The handwriting looks like a default marker font.
The light is a generic product-shot glow with a mirror floor reflection, and there is no texture or atmosphere.
gaps: Commit to one authored world and graphic language across every shot, as B does.
Build the gags into choreographed scenes with layered compositions instead of isolated objects on empty grounds.
Make the type and the palette a deliberate part of the concept, not a default sticky note on mint and cream.

defects: The two forest frames (2 and 3) are almost the same image. The traveller barely moves across the frame, a near-static walk cycle with only a pole drifting through the foreground over roughly 3 s, which reads as dead air.
The lantern beam is a hard-edged, flat-filled triangle. Its long sides have no falloff, so the light looks pasted on rather than cast. Only the far end and the inside have soft, grainy texture.
The eye opens as a thin horizontal sliver: a flat shape-layer scale on the Y axis with no lid, skin or squash, so the creature has no organic quality.

The opening and closing wides use nearly the same layout and the same 'hill + moon' lockoff. The camera does little more than hold, and the moon jumps in size and position between shots without any motivation.
The title type is a generic script serif. 'Woke' is set in a dimmer tint, which is a fade and not a mapped property. The title sits top-left with no relationship to the head reveal.
The snow particles are uniform white dots with soft blobs on top, at a single scale and speed. There is no depth layering, so they flatten the parallax.
The creature's head reveal on the final wide is a cutout silhouette that slides up. It has no anticipation, no weight in the hill mass and no follow-through in the trees.

Audio: evenly spaced click transients (about 0.3 s apart) with pure sine tones under them, then a static noise bed and a broadband wash from 10.2 s. This is thin synthetic material that doesn't line up with the cuts; the clicks keep going through the forest shot without matching the footfalls.
gaps: Motion has no energy curve. Three long, nearly static holds (wide, walk, wide) and a single reveal at the very end leave no build at 60–80%. The hill waking should be animated with anticipation, a rumble, the trees shedding snow, overlap in the mass and a settle, not a cutout that rises.

Sound is placeholder-level. Uniform synthetic ticks and sine pads, with no Foley for footsteps in snow, no wind, no low-end rumble or breath for the hill, and no hit when the eye opens or the head rises. Nothing in the soundtrack is cut to picture.

The finish relies on flat vector silhouettes and noise grain. Light lacks real falloff (hard-edged beam, flat moon glow), the snow has a single depth layer, and the character has no rim light or interaction with the lantern. Top studios would light the volume, add atmospheric depth and sell scale.
